tier_reason: Upgraded C to A: the README ratios come from Google Benchmark result files committed in bench/results/ (v2.0.0, 2026-10-04) produced by the public bench/bench_str.cpp, each naming the CPU (Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4) and exact compiler (Clang 22.0.0 with libstdc++ and libc++, GCC 15.2.0, clang-cl 22.1.0, MSVC 19.44.35213, Emscripten Clang 22), with flags from the public CMakePresets.json Release presets (lzbench public-Makefile precedent). The result files do not name the preset; Release is inferred from the presets and the absence of Google Benchmark's DEBUG warning.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README headline 'Speed up your work with strings by 2-10 times!'. v2.0.0 result files, six toolchains on Xeon E5-2682 v4 (derived from page data): string + number + literal into std::string 1.55-2.46x vs std::to_string concatenation (3.0-5.0x into simstr::stringa), README says 1.6-2x; hex formatting into std::string 4.3-9.2x vs s1 + std::format("{:#x}") + literal (5.9-11.0x into stringa), README says 9-14x, but only 1.3-2.4x vs the std::to_chars version in the same suite; find of three concatenated strings 1.7-3.3x with strexpr into std::string and 3.7-9.7x with stack-buffer lstringa, README says 1.5-9x; conditional concatenation (prec 10) 1.85-3.1x into std::string and 2.1-5.4x into stringa, README says 1.5-2.2x; replace-while-copying 1.4-2.2x, README says 1.5x and higher; split and parse 1.4-3.25x (1.4-1.8x on Linux, 1.8-3.25x on Windows and WASM), README says 2-3x.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 22.0.0 (libstdc++ and, via -stdlib=libc++, libc++) and GCC 15.2.0 on Ubuntu 22 under WSL; clang-cl 22.1.0 and MSVC 19.44.35213 on Windows 10; Emscripten Clang 22 (libc++, 32-bit WASM, -msimd128 -msse4.2 -msse3) run in Chrome 143. CMake Release presets from CMakePresets.json (CMake defaults -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC/Clang, /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG plus /utf-8 /Zc:strictStrings for MSVC), C++23, no -march; Google Benchmark 1.9.4, 4 repetitions, ASLR enabled. The result files do not name the preset used.
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2682 v4 (32 threads at about 2.5 GHz, 40 MiB L3), Windows 10 and Ubuntu 22 under WSL; WASM build in Chrome 143 on the same machine
corrections.caveats: Speedups are against the author's own std idioms (std::to_string or std::format concatenation with temporaries, find + substr + strtol, a hand-written std replace loop), not the fastest std alternatives: with std::to_chars the hex-formatting gap shrinks from 4.3-9.2x to 1.3-2.4x, and in decimal int parsing std::from_chars trails simstr's to_int by only 1.3-1.8x on Linux and beats it under MSVC (11.9 ns vs 15.5 ns). The README's 9-14x hex and 2-3x split figures overstate the v2.0.0 result files (4.3-9.2x and 1.4-3.25x). Not every row wins: hashStrMapA is slightly slower than std::unordered_map<std::string> on Linux (3.73 ms vs 3.64 ms for Clang/libstdc++) and faster only on Windows, and ssa::find ties std::string_view::find on Linux. All runs are on one CPU (Xeon E5-2682 v4), the Linux rows ran under WSL, ASLR was on and only 4 repetitions were taken. The result files do not name the CMake preset (Release inferred). The optional CHECK_RESULT answer checks are compiled out by default, though the split benchmark's std and simstr versions compute the same total by design. bench_str.cpp also compares StringZilla and fmt, which are not baselines here.

notes: Real entry with fair-looking Google Benchmark harness (DoNotOptimize on inputs and outputs, same task on both sides) and committed v2.0.0 result files for six toolchains, so tier rises C to A. Shortcomings to record: README overstates hex (9-14x vs 4.3-9.2x measured) and split (2-3x vs 1.4-3.25x); baselines are naive std idioms (std::to_chars narrows hex to 1.3-2.4x); hashStrMapA not faster than std::unordered_map on Linux; single CPU, WSL Linux runs, preset not named in result files. orefkov.github.io/simstr/results.html was EGRESS_BLOCKED, but bench/results.html and the raw result files in the repo carry the same data.
